Nicolas Tugui, Shahinur Islam, and Daniel Heath developed in 2026 high throughput tests for how salmon and their relatives respond to salt stress at the gene level. Salmonids move between fresh and salt water, and their bodies must remodel to handle each, a process called osmoregulation. When that adjustment is stressed, by farming conditions or warming rivers, gene activity reveals the strain early.

The authors built assays that read those gene responses across several species at once and assessed how well the tests perform. Hatcheries and conservation programs could use such tools to check fish welfare and readiness for sea transfer without waiting for visible harm. The work also supports comparisons of how different salmonid species cope with changing waters.
pmc-13122013:
Mubeena Javed leads a 2026 systematic review on treating EGFR-mutated lung cancer that has spread to the brain. EGFR is a growth signal receptor, and cancers with its faulty form respond to targeted blocker drugs called TKIs. Brain spread affects a large share of these patients and complicates care.

Twenty-seven studies covering nearly fifteen thousand patients were included. Newer third-generation blockers, including osimertinib, worked well inside the brain. Adding radiation improved local control and survival in selected patients, mainly those with few brain spots and moderate to severe symptoms. Focused radiation preserved thinking better than whole-brain radiation. Choice should weigh tumor load and patient condition, the authors conclude.
pmc-13186413:
Peter Edlund, Alfons Gronstrom, and Ulrika Winblad examine private primary care providers in Sweden in a 2026 article. Since the early nineteen nineties, Scandinavian politicians have used market-style reforms to attract diverse private actors into public services. Sweden went furthest, hoping for savings and better quality. The authors mapped all public and private primary care providers in twenty twenty-four.

Private providers ran close to half of all centers. Yet diversity was low on all three dimensions checked. Most private centers were limited companies, nearly all ran for profit, and most relied on bank loans for outside funding. The authors call the pattern a problem for reformers who wanted varied organizational forms.
pmc-13197413:
Maryam Davani and colleagues present a 2026 model that reads heart tracings to sort heart disease. An ECG records the heart's electrical signal. Its wavy, nonlinear shape defeats simple methods, so the team built a hybrid of fuzzy logic, which handles graded rules, and a neural network.

Heart signals from a public database were cleaned and turned into images. A nature-inspired search tuned the images and the model settings. The model sorted beats into seven classes set by a clinical standard. It scored near ninety-nine point seven percent accuracy in their tests. Detection of two risky beat types tied to sudden death improved most. The authors say the model beat several standard rivals.
pmc-13211313:
Reading a molecule's structure from its magnetic spectra is expert work, and a 2026 study by Chao Han automates it with vision transformers. The research article introduces NMRViT, which takes raw one- and two-dimensional NMR spectrum images directly, instead of hand-picked peak lists, and predicts the molecular structure end to end.

Training ran on a large simulated spectral library before testing on real experimental benchmarks. Moving from simulation to the laboratory left a clear performance gap, but fine-tuning on a handful of real spectra shrank it substantially in the authors' experiments. A final re-ranking step, scoring candidates against expected chemical shifts, lifted accuracy in both settings.
pmc-13237113:
Gmelin and colleagues run a genome-wide study of short repeating DNA stretches in Alzheimer's disease. Most such studies scan single letter changes and skip these repeats, called short tandem repeats, though repeats can switch genes on or off. The team tested repeats across the genomes of about a third of a million people in the UK Biobank.

Their group included a few thousand Alzheimer's cases, many more people classed by family history as likely cases, and a large control group. Repeats were read both from gene-chip guesses and from full genome sequencing. Hits from this overlooked layer of DNA could reveal fresh mechanisms behind a disease that still lacks a clear genetic story.
pmc-13241413:
Ng's team at Flinders University compared telehealth use between Australians with and without cancer. National Patient Experience Surveys from 2022 to 2024 supplied the data. Respondents numbered over two thousand with cancer and 45 thousand without. Logistic models mapped who used telehealth and what followed.

Thirty-eight percent of cancer respondents had used telehealth, against 26 percent of others. Mental health conditions raised use in both groups, while being uninsured or less educated lowered it. Cancer patients using telehealth reported the poorest health and most hospital contact, reflecting greater need. Over ninety percent of users rated the service positively.
pmc-13241513:
Elkhoriby and colleagues at Mansoura University fed plant additives to two strains of Japanese quail and tracked growth and gene activity. Three hundred young female quails entered the trial, split evenly between brown and white strains. Each strain received a plain control diet or drinking water dosed with frankincense or lemon balm extract. The feeding period lasted twenty-eight days.

Responses depended strongly on strain, a clear interaction between genetics and treatment. Frankincense at both tested levels suited the brown strain best. For white quails, the lower frankincense level and the stronger lemon balm dose worked best. Treated birds gained weight more efficiently and switched on growth and antioxidant genes while quieting a muscle-limiting gene.
pmc-13242113:
Neven and colleagues in Antwerp correct their systematic review of recessive congenital methemoglobinemia, a rare inherited blood disorder. The review catalogued reported cases and their CYB5R3 gene variants. Two production errors slipped into the printed version. An author's name was also printed incorrectly.

Tables 2 and 3 had been switched, sending readers to the wrong tables from three spots. Table 2 covers diagnostic tests and therapy; Table 3 lists the unique gene variants. The garbled byline is fixed to Marije Meuwissen. Treatment details in the review stand: most documented patients got vitamin C, some with methylene blue. The original article has been updated accordingly.
pmc-13242513:
Mona Hegazy and co-authors tested a diabetes drug as a partner for the standard treatment of schistosomiasis in mice. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Praziquantel kills the Schistosoma mansoni worms, but liver damage from the infection often persists, so helpers are needed. Infected mice received dapagliflozin alone or combined with praziquantel, and the team counted worms and eggs and examined liver tissue under the microscope.

The combination clearly outperformed the untreated course of infection. Worm burden and liver egg load fell, more of the remaining eggs were mature or dead, and the granulomas that scar the liver grew fewer and smaller. Protective liver chemicals rose, and a marker of programmed cell death increased as well. Used alone, dapagliflozin also showed benefit, though the pairing looked strongest. The authors propose it as a convenient add-on that targets inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death together.
pmc-13244513:
Yue Xi and colleagues built a prediction model for metabolic syndrome in women around menopause, centered on a simple body shape measure. Their study appeared in Annals of Medicine in 2026. The body roundness index, computed from height and waist, estimates visceral fat better than weight alone. Models were trained on United States survey data from 2007 to 2020, checked in a Chinese hospital cohort, and extended with a ten-year follow-up.

A neural network won the cross-sectional contest, scoring about 0.85 on internal testing and 0.88 externally, with sound calibration. Importance ranking put body roundness at the very top of sixteen predictors, ahead of liver enzymes and blood cell measures. Adding how roundness and lab values drift over years sharpened the long-term forecasts further. The authors offer the tool for screening in clinics where a tape measure is always available. Catching the syndrome early is the prize.
pmc-13247313:
Yaikhan and co-authors analyzed the genomes of a notorious hospital pathogen at global scale in this 2026 Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal study. Acinetobacter baumannii resists many antibiotics, and its resistance genes often travel on mobile DNA such as plasmids and insertion sequences. The team assembled ten and a half thousand quality genomes and asked whether resistance load tracks the mobile element load within each bacterial lineage.

A few lineages dominated the collection. Genome-wide, resistance burden correlated only modestly with insertion-sequence counts and plasmid variety, and a stricter count of genuinely acquired resistance told a similar story. Mobile-element features differed sharply between lineages, while virulence gene profiles stayed comparatively uniform. The authors argue resistance in this pathogen must be understood lineage by lineage, not as one global pattern.
pmc-13247913:
Havers, Fazel, and Smuk mapped how childhood maltreatment and teenage emotional problems intersect across social positions in England, in this 2026 Epidemiology and Psychiatric Sciences study. Average group comparisons hide combined disadvantage. So the team used a multilevel intersectional method on the OxWell 2023 survey. Nearly twenty thousand students aged eleven to sixteen were sorted into one hundred eighty strata. The strata combined gender, ethnicity, poverty, school year, and school deprivation.

Maltreatment's damage was pervasive yet uneven across those strata. Most inequality in emotional problems reflected simply additive social patterning, each disadvantage stacking. But non-additive intersectional effects appeared too, and they were stronger among maltreated adolescents. The authors argue for trauma-informed, equity-focused policy that looks at combinations of disadvantage. Teenagers carrying several disadvantages at once bear distinctive, not merely summed, psychological costs.
pmc-13248113:
Cezar and colleagues built a scoring system for pig diseases in the United States, reported in 2026. Veterinary labs confirm many infections in tissue samples, yet no single ranking showed which causes were most active. The team combined years of records from the Iowa State University diagnostic laboratory into one index.

They analyzed nearly sixty thousand tissue cases covering eighty-one causes, from bacteria and viruses to parasites. The index stayed stable across years, with PRRS virus and Streptococcus suis scoring highest most often. Two less familiar viruses rose over time. The authors offer the index, shown on an interactive dashboard, as a planning tool for disease control.
pmc-13249113:
Roh, Yoon, and Oh tested a sleep chatbot built around questions rather than instructions, reported in 2026. Digital therapy for insomnia teaches proven habits, yet users often drop out because the programs lecture instead of listening. Their SleepPathfinder chatbot asks Socratic questions, then lets users decide their own next step, in a four-stage conversation.

A one-session pilot with forty-five users rated the system usable and credible. In a five-day comparison with thirty users, the questioning style softened how threatening users found their sleep problems and nudged feelings of choice upward. Deeper personal storytelling, not the sheer number of questions, tracked with changed thinking. The authors propose the layer as a companion to standard digital therapy.
pmc-13249713:
Alperen Aksakal and colleagues report a 2026 lung study of young smokers who feel perfectly healthy. Standard breathing tests can look normal early in smoking, even while the smallest airways are already changing, so the team used a gentler sound-wave test that is more sensitive to those airways.

University students who smoked were compared with never-smokers before and after a six-minute walk test. Both groups had similar standard test results, but smokers showed higher airway resistance and stiffer small airways. Smokers also walked less far and had lower oxygen levels in their leg muscles. The authors say the sound-wave test could flag early smoking harm sooner.
pmc-13250213:
Tuyisenge and colleagues reflect on a six-year partnership that worked to improve care for mothers and newborns in Rwanda. Their 2026 BMJ Paediatrics Open paper describes work by British and Rwandan pediatric bodies with UNICEF and Rwanda's health ministry. From 2017 to 2023, the program ran across many hospitals and selected health centers.

The authors report measurable gains in care quality and patient outcomes over the program years. Even so, preventable newborn deaths persisted, which they link to deeper system limits and community-level health factors. They argue that the numbers are only part of the program's value. Working side by side for years also revealed the structural reasons good clinical steps sometimes fail to become reliable care.
pmc-13253713:
Lasse Bohlen and colleagues test machine learning for intensive care in a 2026 study across two health systems. Models were built with data from a German university hospital and the MIMIC-IV database from the United States. The tasks were to predict death, length of stay, and return to hospital for ICU patients.

Models trained on local data beat models brought in from outside when enough local data existed. Simpler and mid-level models, such as additive models, traveled better across hospitals than complex ones. They also needed far less local data, and tools that explain model choices helped show where data gaps hurt results.
pmc-13253813:
Shakila Umer and a large team study plant DNA barcodes in a 2026 paper on the western Himalayas. The region holds many plants found nowhere else, yet its local flora is little studied at the DNA level. The team tested eight barcode regions in 32 endemic and threatened species from Pakistan's western Himalayas.

One marker, rbcL, worked best, with full copying success and 96% sequencing success. Another marker reached full copying but 80% sequencing, while ITS2 lagged at 52%. Database matches were at least 97% alike for most species, supporting barcodes as a tool to name and group these plants.
pmc-13254113:
Sadia Munawar and colleagues build an AI tool for lung tissue diagnosis in a 2026 study. The system uses CLIP, a model that links images with text, to sort lung samples into benign tissue, adenocarcinoma, or squamous cell carcinoma. Tailored text prompts and a loss method that handles uneven class sizes guided training.

Training used thousands of images per class, split for training, checking, and testing. The best check accuracy reached 95.20 percent, with strong curve scores near 0.987. Training stopped early at epoch 23, a full pass through the data, after steady gains. The authors see promise for digital pathology systems.
pmc-13255213:
Jan Stein and colleagues track body temperature in major trauma in a 2026 registry study. Low body temperature is part of a deadly triad in severe injury, but how it changes during early care is less known. The team analyzed 34,877 patients from a German trauma registry between 2015 and 2023.

Low temperature affected 10.7 percent of patients on arrival and 9.7 percent at intensive care transfer. Staying cold throughout carried the highest death rate at 43.5 percent, plus the most clotting problems and transfusions. New cold at transfer also fared badly, with 31.9 percent deaths. The authors urge active temperature tracking and control.
pmc-13256613:
Shevchenko and a local team surveyed drug residues in beef, pork, and animal feed across Kazakhstan's Kostanay region, and tested meat bacteria for drug resistance. Traces were common in all three materials, though every level stayed below legal maximum limits. Levels differed sharply by feed type.

Meat samples carried E. coli and S. aureus, with samples showing moderate to high resistance, strongest in pork. Resistance was highest against tetracycline, streptomycin, and thiamphenicol. The authors warn that even trace residues moving through the feed-to-food chain may sustain selective pressure and spread resistant microbes. They call for thorough checks of feed and animal products.
pmc-13260213:
Zhenbing Ma and colleagues compare starch from zhiqu wheat, grown for liquor starter, with bread wheat starch. The two wheats feed very different crafts, yet their starch architecture was barely contrasted. Their 2026 analysis measures granules, crystals, and cooking behavior side by side.

Zhiqu starch carried slightly less amylose and somewhat larger mid-sized granules. Its crystals packed more orderly, and its pastes thickened higher at peak, trough, and finish. Branching ran lower in the liquor wheat's starch chains. Statistical mapping showed zhiqu quality traits holding unusually steady across samples. Growers choosing varieties for fermentation now have firmer guidance.
pmc-13260813:
Mohamed M Shabib and colleagues present a 2026 numerical study of tuned mass dampers for earthquake protection in twelve-story steel buildings. A tuned mass damper is a heavy mass that sways against a building's motion to cut shaking, without external power. Using nonlinear time-history simulations under scaled earthquake records, the team compared a single damper with multi-damper layouts spread vertically, horizontally, and around the perimeter, in regular and irregular building plans.

For the regular building, a four-corner horizontal layout was tested for mistuning, and a frequency deviation of plus or minus four percent gave the lowest top displacement. For irregular plans shaped like T, C, L, and a stadium, a perimeter multi-damper layout cut maximum top displacement by between 18.3 percent and 52.3 percent, depending on the plan. Torsional rotation fell by between 25.4 percent and 68.0 percent, a large drop in twist, with base shear and acceleration also reduced.
pmc-13262613:
Xiaoxiao Sun and colleagues present a shared resource for studying cancer cells that survive targeted drugs in a 2026 journal article. These persister cells lack stable genetic resistance yet can seed relapse. The resource, called ResMap, offers a standard test setup and a data set so results from different labs can be compared fairly.

The team tested 94 compounds against 57 candidate targets in four lung cancer models, under normal and low oxygen. A first screen found 12 targets with activity across cancer types and oxygen levels, and follow-up work confirmed 9 of them. Some targets worked only in certain settings, including combinations tied to KRAS-driven cancer. Mouse and human cell data added a safety check for ranking targets.
pmc-13262713:
Cornelia M Weyand and Jörg J Goronzy review how ageing reshapes the immune system in a 2026 journal article. The immune network defends against infection and cancer, but stress over a lifetime wears down its structure. The authors trace changes in blood stem cells and in T and B cells, the white blood cells that learn to target specific threats.

Ageing stem cells renew themselves less well and produce skewed mixes of cells, they explain. Learner immune cells lose their fresh, untrained pool, their variety shrinks, and their internal power and stress systems falter. The result is a paradox: weaker defense alongside more chronic inflammation and self-attack. They illustrate this with rheumatoid arthritis and giant cell arteritis, two diseases of older adults.
pmc-13263013:
Annie Reid and co-authors evaluate action planning inside a digital program to cut sugary drink intake in Appalachian adults in a 2026 journal article. The program, iSIPsmarter, pairs online lessons with text-message drink tracking and a connected scale. In most modules, users set goals, name barriers, and pick strategies, then update plans as feedback arrives.

The 119 participants completed most of their drink action plans, and 80 percent finished all five. About half rated carrying out their plans as hard or impossible, a share that stayed steady. At the program's end, 57 percent of remaining users met their drink goal, and 46 percent met the recommended daily limit. Top barriers were caffeine, taste, and habit.
pmc-13263213:
Shejil Kumar and co-authors evaluate a risk-targeted bone fracture service in Sydney in a 2026 journal article. Fracture liaison services find patients after a fragility fracture, a break from weak bones, and start treatment to prevent the next one. In 2018 the service shifted to inviting higher-risk patients first. The team compared outcomes before and after the change in 1,903 patients.

The later cohort was older, had higher estimated ten-year fracture risk, and more often had hip or spine fractures. Treatment with bone drugs started in 79 percent under the new approach, versus about 65 percent before. Modeling estimated the targeted service would prevent more fractures over five years per thousand patients. The authors note adherence and repeat fracture data are still needed.
pmc-13264613:
Song Wang and a large team present a 2026 data paper describing a full simulation data set for ship hydrodynamics, the study of how water flows around hulls. Computer flow simulations, called CFD, take days and yield huge files, yet AI tools lack rich real data to learn from. Most older sets hold only final flow pictures.

The set comes from a Chinese ship research center and covers two tanker ships and a submarine. It holds every stage of the work: design files and test records, the maths systems solved mid-run, and the final flow results with their meshes. The hull shapes create complex, split flows at the stern. The authors aim the set at AI training, solver testing, data management, and flow display research.
pmc-13264813: Jaume Capdevila and a large team published a correction notice in 2026 for the LEVEL trial, a randomized study in patients with neuroendocrine tumors of the lung and thymus. The trial compares a radioactive lutetium drug against everolimus for survival and quality of life. The correction changes only the competing interests statement. It removes the line saying the remaining authors had no competing interests, and adds that one author is a co-founder, stakeholder, and chief medical officer of SILON Therapeutics. The notice states the original article has been updated.
pmc-13264913:
Irene Brusini and co-authors wrote a 2026 protocol for a study testing an AI tool that flags adults whose type 1 diabetes was wrongly labeled type 2. The mix-up delays right treatment and raises the risk of a dangerous crisis called ketoacidosis. The tool was built on national records data and sharpened on regional exchange data, but live proof was missing.

The study will run at two health systems in southeastern Pennsylvania. At the start, the tool will score every adult listed as type 2, using two years of past data. Patients above a set score will go to doctors for chart review and guideline-based follow-up, including antibody tests where fitting. The main measure is how many flagged patients truly have type 1 diabetes. Interviews will probe how doctors adopt and trust the tool.
pmc-13265013:
Xuefei Li and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on a proposed blood marker for rheumatoid arthritis, a long-term autoimmune disease that attacks the joints. Standard markers miss up to a third of patients and lack precision, so combined ratios from routine blood tests draw interest. The letter weighs one such ratio, red cell distribution width divided by albumin.

The ratio pairs a sign of chronic inflammation and oxidative stress with albumin, a protein that falls in inflammation and poor nutrition. Large survey data have tied high values of the ratio to higher death rates in arthritis patients. The letter notes that ratios like this reflect the mixed inflammatory, immune, and metabolic disturbance of the disease. It also flags that a direct head-to-head test of this ratio against other ratios, and of their combined use, remains underexplored.
pmc-13266413:
Aliyi Gerina and two colleagues report a 2026 survey of pharmacy patients at a teaching hospital in Ethiopia. The study checked how happy outpatients were with the Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services system, a national plan for clear, tracked drug services. It covered 326 adults seen from January to March 2024.

Overall, 89 percent of patients said they were satisfied with the pharmacy service. Scores were highest for the space, staff manner, and speed of service. Scores were lower for drug advice, at 75 percent, and for access to medicines. People living in towns were more often satisfied than rural patients.
pmc-13267413:
Zhang and co-authors correct the errors in self-reported diet using blood and urine chemistry. Their 2026 paper works within the Women's Health Initiative cohorts, 108,522 women followed for a median of about sixteen years. Calibration equations for two healthy-eating scores were built from metabolomic profiles, chemical fingerprints of what people actually ate, in feeding and observational substudies.

The equations explained roughly half to three-fifths of the variation in dietary scores, depending on the reporting method. Without calibration, better eating scores were modestly tied to lower colorectal, lung, bladder, and total cancer risk. After calibration, the lung cancer association strengthened markedly, with about 21 percent lower risk per twenty percent higher score, while the total cancer link held. The authors argue metabolomic calibration sharpens diet and cancer research by reducing reporting error.
pmc-13267513:
Hyejeong Lee and Yunmi Lee wrote a 2026 review of copper-based methods for joining nitrogen groups to carbon chains. Aromatic amines, ring-shaped nitrogen compounds, appear in many drugs and advanced materials. Adding an N-H bond across a double bond is a clean way to build them, but these nitrogen partners react weakly and bind metals in tricky ways.

Copper catalysts have recently opened several routes around these problems. The review sorts them into paths that use copper-nitrogen attack, acid-like activation of the chain, and radical steps. Each path gives different control over where the nitrogen lands and which mirror form results. The authors map what governs that control, aiming to guide chemists who design new reactions.
pmc-13269113:
Hussein Akil and co-authors published a review in 2026 of surgery for a slipped disc in the middle back that presses on the spinal cord. The operation reaches the disc from behind and opens the covering of the cord. They weighed nerve recovery against the risks of this route.

Seven studies covering 74 patients were found, with an average age of 52.8 years. Most discs, 70.3 percent, were hardened with calcium. After surgery, 76 percent of patients improved in nerve function, 21 percent stayed stable, and 1.4 percent got worse for good. Fluid leaks from around the cord occurred in 4.1 percent, and no deaths were reported.
pmc-13270413:
Jean Fabrice Yala and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on drug-resistant bacteria in urinary tract infections in Libreville, Gabon. A cross-sectional study ran from October to December 2019 at a military teaching hospital. All patients suspected of urinary infection were included, and isolates were screened for enzyme-based resistance.

Of 295 patients, 54, or 18.3 percent, had confirmed infections, and 74.1 percent of the germs produced broad resistance enzymes. Enterobacter cloacae led at 14.8 percent, followed by E. coli at 11.1 percent. Of 40 such isolates, 87.5 percent were confirmed by gene testing, and nearly half carried at least two resistance genes. All urinary isolates resisted multiple drugs.
pmc-13270913:
Hampus Eksell is lead author of a 2026 comparative study of conservative versus surgical care for fractures of the jaw joint knob, called the mandibular condyle. These fractures are a common jaw injury, affecting men three times as often as women, and the best treatment route is debated.

The team reviewed 281 cases, 144 treated without surgery and 137 with surgery, and gathered long-term symptoms by questionnaire. Surgery was used more in complex cases, such as fractures on both sides. Joint sounds were more common after conservative care, while pain patterns varied by sex and by whether violence caused the injury. Both routes still gave stable bite and pain-free jaw function at similar rates.
pmc-13272213:
Cataldo Procacci is lead author of a 2026 systematic review of biologic therapies for severe asthma, weighing clinical benefit and economic impact together in real-world populations. These targeted antibody drugs have transformed severe asthma care, but combined clinical and cost evidence was incomplete.

Searching two databases for 2014 to 2024 studies, the team kept 27 studies covering 59,958 patients, mostly observational. All drugs cut flare-ups by 46 to 86 percent, hospitalisations fell 57 to 85 percent, and emergency visits fell 52 to 72 percent. Patients dependent on oral steroids dropped by 53 to 67 percent. Savings from reduced care partly offset drug costs, giving favourable cost per flare-up avoided, though the authors flag methodological limits.
pmc-13272913:
Aurore Canoville leads a 2026 study of bone growth in small Dimetrodon species, sail-backed predators from the early Permian period. The German species, Dimetrodon teutonis, is the smallest known and the only one found outside North America. The team used bone tissue analysis and rechecked North American material from four sites.

The German species had thin, poorly supplied bone layers, unlike the thick, richly supplied bone of most North American species. A mature outer layer confirmed it was truly small as an adult, not just young. The authors link its slow, extended growth to seasonal food limits and low predation at its inland site, contrasting with fast growth in North American lowlands.
pmc-13273013:
Shweta Singh and Aqueasha Martin-Hammond present a 2026 participatory design study of voice-enabled AI assistants for older adults and family caregivers. Devices such as Alexa can help with daily health tasks at home. Nine older adults and caregivers took part in eight workshops over four months, imagining future uses.

Participants saw promise in automating daily health tasks, supporting mental well-being, and offering companionship. Yet they felt voice AI alone cannot meet the complex needs of informal care. Concerns raised included transparency, privacy, inclusiveness, trust, affordability, and autonomy. The authors offer design ideas that balance efficiency with these values to support varied caregiving needs and encourage future adoption.
pmc-13274913:
Nadine Domnik and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on building a phone app that shows rehabilitation patients their own health data in plain form. Rehab clinics collect many test results that rarely reach patients in an understandable way. The RehaLink app was co-designed at one rehabilitation center with seventeen inpatients with multiple sclerosis and fifteen health professionals.

Across three feedback rounds, both groups preferred progress bars and color-coded indicators over text-heavy displays. Patients wanted simplicity yet also asked for exact values and comparisons with norms, a tension designers must balance. Professionals underestimated how informative patients wanted the displays to be. Perceived value rose over the study, and usability scores were high, 93.6 from patients and 80.9 from professionals on a hundred-point scale.
pmc-13275613:
Agata Burzawa, Katarzyna Potera, and Aleksandra Walczyńska present a 2026 journal article testing whether diet changes how tiny animals shrink as temperatures rise. Many cold-blooded animals mature smaller when warm, a pattern called the temperature-size rule. The team raised three clones of a rotifer, a microscopic water animal, with different heat preferences, each at four temperatures on three laboratory diets.

Diet changed the pattern, but unevenly across its parts. The lower temperature limit, where growth switches from negative to positive, shifted most with diet. The upper optimum temperature barely moved. The strength of the shrinking response also varied by food. The authors conclude that nutrition can bend thermal growth rules in different directions for different traits, so temperature effects cannot be read off without knowing what the animal eats.
pmc-13276313:
Kai Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on cleaning cadmium from rice paddy soil with charred rice husks. Cadmium, a toxic metal, builds up in farm soils and ends up in rice, threatening food safety. Biochar, a charcoal-like material, can lock metals in place, and chemical treatments may improve it.

The team incubated contaminated soil for one hundred twenty days at four cadmium levels. They compared raw husk biochar with three modified versions, treated with acid, alkali, or an oxidizing agent. The oxidant-treated char held the most acid groups and trapped cadmium best at low to moderate pollution. The alkali-treated char, strongly alkaline, stabilized soil best under severe pollution. Both also shifted soil humus, the dark organic matter tied to fertility. The authors map which char suits which contamination level.
pmc-13276413:
Amanda Morris and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how two bacteria interact in the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis. The thick mucus of this disease hosts chronic infections, often with both Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus together. Patients with both fare worse, but how the species affect each other was unclear.

The three-year study followed forty-five patients with chronic Pseudomonas infection. Microscopy of sputum at flare-ups, after antibiotics, and at recovery mapped both bacteria and a staph protein they release. During flare-ups in children, Pseudomonas volume and cluster count rose, and the two species sat farther apart. Antibiotics shrank small Pseudomonas clusters far more than large ones, which persisted. More staph protein tracked with more Pseudomonas in children. The authors say the species occupy separate niches yet still influence each other.

pmc-13284413:

pmc-13285913:

pmc-13286213:

pmc-13287213:

pmc-13287413:

pmc-13288713:

pmc-13289113:

pmc-13289313:

pmc-13289413:

pmc-13290613:

pmc-13290713:

pmc-13290913:

pmc-13301113:

pmc-13301413:

pmc-13306613:

pmc-13307413:

pmc-13307913:

pmc-13311013:

pmc-13311913:

pmc-13314413:

pmc-13315113:

pmc-13315513:

pmc-13315613:

pmc-13316213:

pmc-13316613:

pmc-13317313:

pmc-13318713:

pmc-13320013:

pmc-13320413:

pmc-13320813:

pmc-13321313:

pmc-13325913:

pmc-13340813:

pmc-13341513:

pmc-13341613:

pmc-13342213:
Kerstin Uvnäs-Moberg and Maria Petersson review, in 2026, how the hormone oxytocin is released and what it does, with close attention to touch, social contact, and closeness. pmc-13342813:

pmc-13344013:

pmc-13346113:

pmc-13347713:

pmc-13348013:

pmc-13348413:

pmc-13352113:

pmc-13352413:

pmc-13352513:

pmc-13354113:

pmc-13354313:

pmc-13354413:

pmc-13355213:

pmc-13356613:

pmc-13357113:

pmc-13359513:

pmc-13360213:

pmc-13361213:

pmc-13361613:

pmc-13362313:

pmc-13362513:

pmc-13364213:

pmc-13364513:

pmc-13375113:

pmc-13380213:

pmc-13382813:

pmc-13383013:

pmc-13383213:

pmc-13385513:

pmc-13386013:

pmc-13389613:

pmc-13389813:

pmc-13390013:

pmc-13412013:

pmc-13412113:

pmc-13412313:

pmc-13414313:

pmc-13417713:

pmc-13418513:

pmc-13418613:

pmc-13419413:

pmc-13420313:

pmc-13421113:

pmc-13421313:

pmc-13421713:

pmc-13421913:

pmc-13422313:

pmc-13422813:

pmc-13423913:

pmc-13424313:

pmc-13424413:

pmc-13424513:

pmc-13424613:

pmc-13425713:

pmc-13426313:

pmc-13426413:

pmc-13426713:

pmc-13427413:

pmc-13428313:

pmc-13431013:

pmc-13435913:

pmc-13436213:

pmc-13437813:

pmc-13438313:

pmc-13438813:

pmc-13439013:

pmc-13439313:

pmc-13440713:

pmc-13446313:
Maruyama and colleagues showed in 2026 that a long first intron, a non-coding stretch inside the PROS1 gene, tunes how much protein S its owner makes across tissues. Protein S helps control blood clotting, and its shortage raises clot risk, yet standard gene tests that read only coding parts miss the cause in about half of affected families. The team probed the intron for regulatory elements in mice and humans.

Elements inside the intron adjusted protein S output in several tissues. Rare variants found there lowered activity in reporter tests, the lab assays that read out a regulatory element's strength. Such variants may explain part of the missing-cause group with protein S deficiency. The authors argue that diagnostic testing should extend into this intron, and that non-coding regulation deserves a routine place in the workup of inherited clotting disorders.
pmc-13446413:
Nelson, McGregor, and Lombrozo test whether stating a belief as a chance, rather than a yes or no, goes with intellectual humility, the habit of owning one's limits and fallibility. A belief framed as a probability admits doubt by design. Their 2026 paper reports two studies: one with 279 students and one with two nationally matched samples of about 270 adults each, covering political and moral beliefs.

Comparing people, the predicted link failed: those who framed more beliefs as chances were not more humble overall, in either sample. Comparing beliefs within the same person, the link appeared. Political and moral beliefs a person held as probabilities came with a humbler stance toward those very beliefs, even after allowing for how extreme the beliefs were. Framing may thus soften single beliefs without marking a humbler character, a hint that teaching chance based framing could cool hard disputes.
pmc-13447113:
Valentina Baderna and colleagues asked what decides how often a gene switch, called an enhancer, is active across a group of cells. Enhancers are DNA stretches that boost nearby genes when proteins called transcription factors bind them.

Using a method that reads single DNA molecules, the team measured how often chromatin, the packed form of DNA, opens at enhancers. Most single factors opened chromatin in only a small share of cells at a time. Added together, though, the binding of many factors set how often an enhancer switched on. Tests on hundreds of enhancers placed at a new genome spot showed the helper protein p300 was needed for full activation.
pmc-13447413:
A S Arya and Rahul Shukla analyse decentralised waste governance in Kerala, India, through a sociological lens in 2026 work. Most waste research focuses on trucks, rules and targets, leaving social effects underexamined. Kerala's Green Task Force model, staffed largely by women who collect sorted waste door to door, offers a rich case for asking how policy shapes everyday environmental roles.

Policy papers, institutional reports and operating guidelines were read with theories of governance, social structure and community trust. Official writing presents the model as building responsibility, participation and inclusion, with women workers gaining new public visibility. Whether daily life matches that picture remains unverified, since no fieldwork tested lived experience. The authors call for on-the-ground research into how households and workers actually experience the system.
pmc-13447813:
Jedidi, Kerkeni, and Ben Lahouel report a 25-year-old man with a painless cystic mass under the skin of his left shoulder blade region. It had grown slowly for five years before he sought care. Scans showed a well-defined cyst measuring about 9 by 5 by 9 centimeters. It sat in the soft tissue over the back ribs, with no cysts in lung or liver.

Blood serology for the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus came back positive. MRI supported a subcutaneous hydatid cyst. A hydatid cyst is a parasitic larval cyst. This soft-tissue form accounts for under 2 percent of hydatid cases. Surgeons excised the cyst completely. Tissue examination confirmed the diagnosis, with its layered germinal membrane visible under the microscope. His recovery was uneventful. He received two 28-day cycles of albendazole separated by a 14-day break, to reduce recurrence risk after surgery.
pmc-13448113:
Kim presents a 2026 editorial on restraint in endoscopic spine surgery, reviving a famous warning. In 1993 an editorial titled 'The Rape of the Spine' accused the field of overusing fusion for financial rather than clinical reasons; a 2015 revisit found little changed. Kim asks whether the fast-growing endoscopic era is destined to repeat that history of enthusiasm outrunning evidence.

Endoscopic techniques are a genuine advance in minimally invasive spine care, shrinking incisions and recovery. But fusion volumes once rose far faster than comparable operations, driven by incentives the editorial names plainly. Kim's imperative of restraint argues that new tools should narrow indications to patients who benefit, not widen them to whoever can be scheduled. The piece is a conscience check for a specialty at the start of its next expansion wave.
pmc-13448213:
Ksenia Anufrieva and colleagues map immune and stromal niches in skin from adults with dermatomyositis in 2026 spatial gene work. The autoimmune disease inflames skin and muscle and carries a strong cancer link, yet which tissue neighbourhoods mark cancer-associated cases was unknown. Comparison with a related skin condition, cutaneous lupus, sharpened what is unique to each disease subtype.

Cancer-linked lesions held scattered immune infiltrates rich in macrophages, or organised lymphoid clusters with dense B cell cores ringed by T cells, while blood vessel structure stayed preserved. Non-cancer skin instead showed dense myeloid infiltrates near injured vessel linings, with signals that drove stromal reshaping and loss of vessel-supporting fibroblasts. Both diseases shared strong interferon signals, while one interferon type appeared only in dermatomyositis skin.
pmc-13449313:
Meiling Chen and colleagues measure in 2026 a metabolic hormone, fibroblast growth factor 21, in the blood of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, asking whether it tracks disease activity and artery health. The study enrolled 187 patients treated at Xuzhou Central Hospital during 2023 and 2024, split by ultrasound into 118 with carotid plaque and 69 without, plus 139 healthy controls. Blood tests covered lipids, insulin resistance, inflammation, arthritis antibodies, and the hormone itself.

Patients carried far higher hormone levels than controls, about 805.7 against 203.8 picograms per milliliter, and those with plaque ran higher still. Levels rose alongside LDL cholesterol, insulin resistance, arthritis antibodies, disease activity scores, and artery wall thickness, and fell with use of disease-modifying drugs. In adjusted models the hormone stood as an independent factor linked to thicker artery walls. The authors propose it as a research marker for cardiovascular risk in this population.
pmc-13449913:
Patcharin Sihathip and co-authors dissect in 2026 a rare hemoglobin variant, Hb Chumphae, found in a Thai man whose anemia was far worse than the usual pattern predicts. The 44-year-old arrived with chronic anemia and an enlarged liver and spleen; his hemoglobin measured just 3.7 grams per deciliter and his red cell distribution width a striking 40.5 percent. Protein separation tests hinted at abnormal hemoglobin peaks, but their patterns mimicked another variant, Hb Bart's, making the true identity easy to miss.

DNA sequencing settled it. A missense change at codon ten swapped valine for aspartic acid in the alpha-globin chain. The same patient also carried the Southeast Asian deletion form of alpha-zero thalassemia. Together, in compound heterozygous state, the pair produced anemia more severe than classic hemoglobin H disease. The team built two DNA tests that can identify the variant directly and mapped its likely ancestral chromosome background.
pmc-13450513:
Zahedi and colleagues test whether a CT measurement can stand in for an invasive ultrasound in judging the heart's most dangerous narrowing. Their 2026 study compares two measures in 45 Iranian patients who had both tests within ninety days. One is the cross-sectional area of the left main coronary artery on CT angiography. The other is the minimal lumen area from intravascular ultrasound. A third had significant narrowing by the ultrasound standard.

The two measurements correlated strongly, at 0.93 across patients. A CT cut-off of about 6.2 square millimetres identified significant stenosis with about 96 percent diagnostic accuracy. Specificity was perfect in this cohort. Nobody above the threshold was misclassified as diseased. Sensitivity was about 88 percent. The authors present CT area as a reliable non-invasive metric for left main assessment and offer the threshold, derived in an Iranian population, for wider validation.
pmc-13450613:
Shengli Shi and co-authors hunt in 2026 for savory taste fragments in cod skin, a fish plant leftover that is often thrown away. Umami, the savory taste, comes from tiny protein pieces that switch on taste buds. The team broke cod skin down with enzymes and sifted the mix by size.

Taste panels and lab tools narrowed the field to five candidate fragments. Computer models then tested how each fragment docks with the umami taste switch on the tongue. One fragment stood out as strongly savory, while two others boosted the taste of a mix. The work gives food makers a path to natural taste boosters from fish waste.
pmc-13451813:
Esben Schroeder and co-authors present in 2026 a partly automated flow for counting and mapping cell cores along single muscle fibers. Hand counts of these cores are slow and prone to bias, which limits big studies of muscle change. Their flow pairs free image tools with custom code to read stained fiber images.

The code logs each core's place, shape, and tilt in three planes, plus its gaps to the fiber spine and to its nearest neighbors. Results roll up per fiber and per biopsy, joined with measures from a second imaging suite. The team offers the flow as a fast, repeatable base for large fiber data sets in muscle labs.
pmc-13451913:
Paula Timonen and co-authors survey in 2026 how Finnish drug stores took up digital and remote services in the first COVID-19 wave. Owners of all private community pharmacies in Finland were polled in late 2020, and 175 replied. Readiness to adopt new ways was scored with a known innovation scale, and stores were split into early and late adopters.

Remote services grew fast: medicine pickup lockers near doubled in share, and online sales rose by a third. Early adopters, about two fifths of stores, offered a wider digital range. Younger owners and high-volume stores showed more readiness. The authors link readiness to service growth, while noting the low reply rate may flatter the picture.
pmc-13452413:
A Ita Juwita and five co-authors test how place of origin and post harvest handling shape Liberica coffee beans from Indonesia. Their 2026 study compares beans from Jambi, Kayong, and Meranti, each handled by the natural dry method or the honey method. Liberica is a less common coffee species that draws growing trade interest across Southeast Asia.

Where a bean grew mattered most, shifting nearly every trait the team measured, while handling mainly changed moisture, fat parts, and antioxidant strength. Jambi honey beans held the most alkaloids, and Kayong natural beans held the most diterpenes, two groups of active plant chemicals. Meranti natural beans carried the most of a key acid group and showed the strongest antioxidant action. Growers can use the map of place and method to aim beans at buyers with set tastes.
pmc-13453013:
Yi Jiang and seven co-authors review ferroptosis, a cell death path driven by iron and fat damage, and its role in heart and vessel disease. Their 2026 review spans clogged arteries, aneurysms, valve disease, heart attack damage, and heart failure. The team lays out how the death path works, what controls it, and which drugs can block it.

Several drug types protected the heart and vessels in animal studies, among them iron binding drugs such as deferoxamine and deferiprone. Antioxidants such as vitamin E and lipoic acid also helped, as did a blocker named Ferrostatin-1. Natural products joined the list of agents that tame the iron driven damage. The authors frame the review as a map for turning these lab finds into new heart treatments.
pmc-13454113:
Kang Li and five co-authors map two decades of research joining childhood obesity with precocious puberty, the early onset of puberty. Their 2026 study pulls 2,506 papers from three databases across 2005 to 2025, written by 9,843 authors in 664 journals. Mapping tools chart output by country, center, and keyword, while a topic model sorts the themes on its own.

Output rose steadily, with the United States and China as the top contributors and Harvard the top center. The most prolific author logged 42 papers, and one pediatric endocrine journal led the venue list. The topic model found 15 themes in four clusters, from adrenal and puberty biology to the body wide damage of childhood obesity. The authors offer the map to help clinicians spot hot spots and new fronts in the field.
pmc-13454313:
Damico, Mathus, and Demchenko tackle a core problem in sugar chemistry in 2026: steering new bonds between sugars to face the right way. Their method uses a hydrogen bond, a weak pull between atoms, to deliver the partner sugar to one side of the growing chain. They built three donor sugars that differ only in where a helper group, called Pico, sits on the ring. They then tested each donor against a range of acceptor sugars.

All three donors gave good to high yields, but the bond direction hinged on Pico placement. Donors with Pico at the third or sixth position favored one link type. Pico at the fourth position favored the other, though less cleanly. The sixth position donor gave complete control in every test. The team then used it to build a four unit chain of amino sugars, with every step fully controlled.
pmc-13457813:
Shaofeng Ma and colleagues traced how a circular RNA molecule helps cervical cancer cells grow and spread. Circular RNAs are loop-shaped RNA molecules that resist breakdown, and one called hsa_circ_0000231 was scarce in healthy cells but plentiful in most cervical cancer cell lines tested. In their 2026 study, the team added extra copies of the molecule to some cancer cells and silenced it in others, then measured growth, movement, and cell death.

Extra circular RNA made the cancer cells proliferate, migrate, and invade faster while reducing programmed cell death, and silencing it reversed all of those effects. The molecule works by teaming with a stabilizing protein, IGF2BP2, to protect the message for a calcium-channel gene named CACNA1H from decay inside the cell. Preserving that message switched on the MAPK growth pathway, and blocking CACNA1H canceled the circular RNA's tumor-promoting effects.
pmc-13458913:
He and Liu comment on a study of isolated dissection of the superior mesenteric artery, a tear in the gut's main artery that can starve the bowel. Doctors sort such tears with imaging based classification systems to guess who will fail watchful care and need a stent. Ling and colleagues compare eight systems head to head in 156 patients from three centers, the largest such test so far.

Tan's system won, adding tear length over five centimeters and severe narrowing of the true channel to the score. Yet He and Liu press a deeper point: every system grades the vessel, not the bowel it feeds, and all rest on the unproven claim that narrowing predicts bowel damage. Past cases show symptoms easing while scans worsen, and even a fully blocked artery with no bowel injury at all. Future systems, they argue, must measure gut viability directly.
pmc-13459113:
Dandan Bi and colleagues review in 2026 how viruses living in the gut shape regulatory T cells, the immune cells that keep inflammation in check. The gut virome includes bacteriophages, which attack bacteria, and viruses that infect our own cells. The review separates two routes of influence: an indirect route running through bacteria and their chemical products, and a direct route where viral patterns trigger immune sensors.

That dual framing helps explain how the virome can protect gut balance in health yet feed disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease when it shifts. Effects may also reach beyond the gut into body-wide immune conditions. The authors discuss virome measures as possible diagnostic markers and treatment targets, while stressing how much mechanism remains unsettled.
pmc-13459213:
Lordina Amoah and co-authors investigated whether a stronger financial system can blunt the health damage climate change causes across Africa. Their 2026 study assembled panel data for 43 African countries spanning 2000 to 2023 and used a dynamic statistical method suited to country level time series. Health was measured through life expectancy and mortality rates, climate through carbon emissions, and finance through an index of financial development. That let the team test direct effects and whether finance softens the climate effect.

Higher carbon emissions shortened life expectancy and raised mortality across the sample. Financial development worked the other way, lengthening life expectancy and reducing mortality. Crucially, the analysis showed finance also weakened the harmful link between emissions and health outcomes. The authors advise governments to invest in climate resilient clinics, clean water, and disease monitoring, and urge financial firms to build products like weather indexed insurance.
pmc-13459913:
Pelin Karaçay and co-authors measured AI literacy among Turkish nursing students and asked what raises it. Their 2026 national study surveyed 383 undergraduates with a standard literacy scale. It then explored students' own views of AI in interviews and open responses. Participants averaged about twenty one years old, and more than four in five were women.

The average literacy score was 110.80 on the scale, with technical understanding the strongest subscale at 41.22 in the reported breakdown. Analysis tied higher literacy most strongly to personal comfort with new technologies. Having witnessed ethical concerns about AI came second, and both links held up. Seven themes captured student attitudes, from convenience and time savings to fears of misinformation, dependency, and laziness. Nursing curricula should build hands on comfort while teaching ethical scrutiny, the authors argue.
pmc-13460213:
Satoshi Fumimoto and colleagues explored in 2026 whether spread through air spaces predicts recurrence along the staple line after wedge removal of colorectal cancer that has spread to the lung. In this pattern, tumor cells drift into air pockets beyond the main mass. Seventy patients with seventy lesions were treated at a Japanese university hospital between 2011 and 2020. Each lesion was reviewed for spread status, surgical margin, and the ratio between tumor and margin size.

Spread appeared in about a quarter of lesions, and recurrence at the staple line in a fifth. In simple analysis, spread showed only a suggestive trend, while margin measures were significant. In the combined exploratory model, both spread and the tumor-to-margin ratio stayed associated with recurrence. The authors frame their findings as hypothesis-building for wider resections where spread is found.
pmc-13460313:
Sergio A. Acuna and colleagues compared in 2026 two warm-perfusion strategies for liver transplants from donors whose hearts had stopped, using national United States transplant data from 2022 to 2024. Such livers historically suffered bile duct injury from oxygen starvation. One strategy perfuses the donor's abdominal organs in place, the other perfuses the liver on a machine after removal, and each was compared against rapid recovery with cold storage across 4,632 transplants.

Machine perfusion after rapid recovery and regional perfusion with cold storage each cut graft loss substantially versus the old standard, and the two modern strategies matched each other. Adding machine perfusion after regional perfusion brought no extra benefit. The authors endorse both approaches as complementary parts of a new standard for these donors.
pmc-13461413:
Qiujie Zhang, Zhaoxi Han, and Qinghui Peng surveyed in 2026 Chinese nursing home caregivers to untangle how workplace social capital, the trust and support among colleagues, relates to wanting to quit. Their cross-sectional sample held 222 caregivers. The model tested burnout as the bridge between social resources and turnover intention, with professional certification as a possible modifier. It drew on social capital and resource conservation theories.

Richer workplace social capital came with weaker intention to leave, and burnout carried part of that link statistically. Certification changed the pathway: the burnout bridge held only for uncertified caregivers, while certified staff showed no significant indirect link. The authors suggest facilities invest in team cohesion especially for uncertified workers, whose personal resources are thinnest.
pmc-13461613:
John von Freyend and colleagues reported in 2026 a life-saving decision to start chemotherapy before a cancer diagnosis was confirmed by tissue tests. A 35-year-old man arrived with massive testicular swelling, severe breathlessness, swollen legs, and kidney failure. Scans showed widespread spread to the lungs and the back of the abdomen, plus pneumonia. He needed a ventilator, continuous kidney support, and blood pressure drugs in intensive care.

Freyend's team judged the picture fit a metastatic germ cell tumor, backed by raised tumor markers in his blood. They began a three-drug regimen one day after arrival, before tissue proof. He improved clearly after one cycle, and later surgery on the testicle confirmed residual seminoma. Later cycles needed dose cuts for kidney damage, infections, and heart strain, and one drug was dropped for severe side effects. Final scans showed overall tumor shrinkage with residual spots.
pmc-13461713:
Wang and colleagues pooled in 2026 the evidence on blood inflammation markers for predicting outcomes in upper tract urothelial carcinoma, a cancer of the kidney's urine channel and ureter. Patients face surgery that removes the kidney and ureter, and sorting who will fare badly is hard. The team gathered twelve studies covering 7,346 patients and five markers, all simple ratios or indices built from routine blood counts taken before surgery.

Wang found higher levels of every marker went with worse survival overall. The strongest pooled link for overall survival came from the systemic inflammation response index, which roughly doubled the risk of death. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio showed a similar near-doubling with tight agreement between studies. Cancer-specific and freedom-from-return results pointed the same way. The authors warn the markers were pooled separately, with differing cut-offs, so no ranking between them is justified yet.
pmc-13462413:
Kerstin Denecke and Elia Gabarron studied how accuracy, tone, and disclaimers shape trust in medical advice given by AI chatbots. They surveyed 115 people, who judged chatbot answers across 15 scenarios covering five common health problems.

Accuracy proved the strongest driver of trust, yet participants still failed to spot wrong advice in many cases. Tone mattered little: chatbots sounded confident to users whether their wording was bold or tentative. Disclaimers nudged people toward second opinions only in some scenarios, with effects that swung by case. Denecke concludes that disclaimers alone cannot stop over-reliance, so chatbots must state their limits plainly and push users to check advice.
pmc-13462513:
Donghui Ren, Yufang Qu, and Hui Sun argue, in a 2026 perspective article, that digital health tools should be designed around health workers' sleep, bodies, and workload. They should not be added on top of broken systems. Tired staff, ruined sleep, and clumsy software threaten worker health and hospital resilience. The authors treat those harms as design failures, not as weak personal resilience.

Their proposed human-centered ecosystem puts staffing, shift schedules matched to body clocks, protected rest, and supportive conditions first. Only then may artificial intelligence help, acting as a shield that ranks, merges, or filters low-value information. Tool rollouts should be staged, co-designed with staff, and watched for shifting work onto others. Success should be judged by after-hours work, mental load, recovery, and fairness, not just speed. The core claim: digital change should remove avoidable work, never paper over fixable faults.
pmc-13464013:
Hammers and colleagues tested a two-gene therapy in 2026 for the heart failure that kills most people with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The disease is the inherited muscle-wasting condition of boys. A severe mouse model hosted the tests. Genes for two proteins, S100A1 and ARC, were delivered into heart muscle by a virus-based carrier, separately and combined. S100A1 handles calcium, and ARC protects cells from dying.

Each gene helped differently. S100A1 improved the heart's ability to relax and fill. ARC kept animals alive longer. Combined in one vector, the pair improved long-term heart function and tissue health. The pair even softened heart failure triggered by a partial dystrophin replacement gene. The team showed the combined therapy could be delivered safely through the coronary arteries in a dog model. With a muscle-wide promoter, the same package strengthened skeletal muscle too.
pmc-13464913:
Wan-Hua Ting and five co-authors test belly-cavity chemotherapy for first-return ovarian cancer in a small early study. Standard care gives platinum drugs plus a wrapped doxorubicin form through the vein. Their plan dosed the drugs straight into the belly cavity as well, aiming at the disease where it spreads.

Thirteen patients took the repeat cavity treatment and were compared with vein-only patients from records. Tolerance matched the standard route, with no extra safety burden standing out. About eighty-five percent of cavity patients saw tumors shrink, and the middle time before growth resumed ran near fourteen months. The authors call the approach feasible for chosen patients and press for a proper prospective trial.
pmc-13465013:
Muamer Dizdar leads a team that compares a seven-form magnesium supplement against single magnesium forms in rats. Magnesium feeds hundreds of body reactions, yet its chemical forms may act quite differently. Sixty-day-old male rats took the blend or oxide, citrate, or glycinate forms by stomach tube for thirty days.

The blend raised blood magnesium without disturbing blood sugar handling. Brain tissue showed shifts in synapse proteins tied to learning flexibility, and gene activity for BDNF, a growth signal, also moved. Rats on the blend showed mild calming in behavior tests with no change in movement. Kidney and liver tissue stayed clean under the microscope, and effects overall matched the single forms dose for dose.
pmc-13466513:
Chen and colleagues build a knowledge graph mapping how genes are regulated in specific brain cell types, in 2026 biology data research. Such evidence lies scattered across papers using clashing cell-type names. Their graph standardizes cell types with a three-level taxonomy of 79 categories anchored to the Cell Ontology. It adds molecular fingerprints from two large human brain single-cell datasets covering over 4 million cells, and mines published abstracts for curated regulatory evidence records.

A language model kept 25,812 evidence records, and the graph holds 41,532 directed relationships between genes, regulators, and cell types. For prediction tests, the team exported a cleaned subgraph of 19,819 triples spanning 10,660 entities. That model can rank possible regulators and markers for a given cell type, demonstrated on microglia, the brain's immune cells. Chen offers the graph as shared groundwork for comparing brain regulation studies.
pmc-13466813:
Emel Özalp and colleagues ask which egg follicle size at trigger shot gives the best odds in letrozole fertility treatment with insemination, in a 2026 study. The analysis covered 596 treatment cycles from 454 women under forty treated across fifteen months. Cycles were grouped by the leading follicle's width: under nineteen millimeters, nineteen to twenty-one, and above twenty-one.

Pregnancy and live birth rates peaked in the middle band, where live births reached about fifteen percent against a small fraction in the smallest band. Adjusted odds clearly favored the middle size, though the ranges around those odds ran wide. Models accounted for women contributing several cycles, so one person's repeats could not skew the answer.
pmc-13467113:
Piotr Kowalski and colleagues describe a one-position operation that corrects a teenager's congenital spinal curve without ever turning him over, in a 2026 surgical report. The fifteen-year-old's chest spine curved from a butterfly-shaped vertebra at the tenth level, and bracing had failed. Lying on his side throughout, he first received screws placed through the skin from mid-back to lower spine under X-ray guidance.

Surgeons then reached the spine from the side, sparing muscle and passing behind the chest lining, to remove part of the malformed vertebra unevenly and straighten the column. Brain and cord signals were monitored throughout. The single-position plan trims the repositioning and much of the tissue damage of older multi-approach corrections.
pmc-13467513:
Ameen Nasser and colleagues review in 2026 the drug tafamidis for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, a disease where a misshapen protein builds up in the heart and steadily weakens it. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 rules and searched three major databases through March 2026 for studies of adults on the drug. Outcomes of interest ranged from heart scans and blood markers to walking ability, death rates, and safety.

Seventeen studies covering 1,890 patients met the criteria. Because the studies differed too much to pool numerically, the authors summarized them in narrative form. Tafamidis was linked with steadier heart strain measures, preserved daily functioning, and lower overall mortality in the reports reviewed. The synthesis gives clinicians a current map of what the drug appears to do and where the data stay thin.
pmc-13467913:
Sarah Ammar Al Dhamin, Dalia AlDhamin and Zaed Jaber published this 2026 review on skin and mucosal signs as early warnings of internal disease. Because the skin, mouth and eyes are easy to examine, their changes can betray autoimmune, infectious, metabolic, hormonal and cancerous conditions before other symptoms declare themselves. The authors searched five databases and references for findings with diagnostic weight, sorting them by the body systems they point to.

Classic examples carry diagnostic weight: the malar rash and mouth ulcers of lupus, and the heliotrope rash and Gottron papules of dermatomyositis. Infections announce themselves too, with oral thrush and hairy leukoplakia in HIV and the mucous patches and palm-and-sole rash of syphilis. Darkened velvety skin and eruptive fatty bumps flag insulin resistance and lipid disorders, while several rashes, including acquired fish-scale skin, can precede an internal cancer diagnosis. The review stresses pattern recognition in clinical context.
pmc-13468113:
Buren Li, Ayat Yaseen, and Nikola P Pavletich reveal in 2026, at near-atomic resolution, how the protein TOPBP1 switches on the ATR checkpoint kinase that guards DNA replication. When replication forks stall, ATR and its partner ATRIP must fire the S-phase checkpoint, and TOPBP1 is essential for that induction. How its activating domain wakes the kinase up was not understood. The team froze the human protein complex and imaged it with cryo-electron microscopy.

The structure, resolved at 3.0 angstroms, shows the TOPBP1 domain binding far from the active site yet forcing a global shape change that realigns the catalytic residues about 70 angstroms away. A second structure with the other activator, ETAA1, showed it grips the kinase in a distinctly different mode. The contrast helps explain why the two activators run different branches of checkpoint signaling, one for stalled forks and one for normal cell cycle timing.
pmc-13468813:
Puigdueta and co-authors review the case for miR-7 in brain disease, in this 2026 article. MiR-7 is a tiny RNA molecule that fine-tunes gene activity. The molecule is abundant in the central nervous system. It is also unusually well conserved across species. It touches energy metabolism, inflammation, oxidative stress, and neuron survival all at once.

The review gathers evidence linking miR-7 to neurodegenerative, neurological, and psychiatric disorders, arguing it acts as a molecular node where metabolic imbalance converts into nervous-system dysfunction. Separate sections trace its confirmed gene targets and the pathways they control, then weigh its promise as a biomarker and treatment target. The authors' central point is that miR-7's reach extends well beyond metabolic regulation. It was first known for that narrower role. Therapies aimed at it could thus influence several disease processes at once.
pmc-13470213:
Jordan and co-authors built a 2026 gene model for the fruit fly Drosophila arawakana, mapping its version of a gene called CG31087. An ortholog is the matching gene in another species, and this one belongs to a detoxification gene family. The work feeds a comparative study of how that family evolved across a fly lineage.

Working from a public genome assembly, Jordan compared the gene's neighbourhood in both fly species to check that matching genes sit in matching order. The gene lies on opposite DNA strands in the two species, a detail the model records carefully. Prediction programmes and RNA sequencing reads from adult flies supported the model's coding regions. The annotation was produced through an undergraduate research course partnership in genomics education.
pmc-13471513:
Mohamed and co-authors report a previously healthy 15-year-old girl who developed optic neuritis, inflammation of the optic nerve, in both eyes shortly after HPV vaccination. Their 2026 case report describes painful vision loss in the right eye beginning seven days after a quadrivalent HPV shot, with two weeks of symptoms before presentation.

Examination found a marked mismatch in sharpness between the eyes and a right-sided pupillary defect, while other cranial nerves and motor, sensory, and balance checks stayed normal. The hard part was separating a post-vaccine immune reaction from early multiple sclerosis or neuromyelitis optica, diseases that can open with the same picture. Optic neuritis is the first sign in about 20% of multiple sclerosis patients. The authors stress careful, methodical exclusion before blaming the vaccine.
pmc-13472513: Person-centred care puts patients' individual needs first, but what does that mean for the managers running a hospital ward? Drawing on interviews at a private hospital, this study captures how frontline nurse managers view and practice person-centred management. Their perspectives reveal how the philosophy translates, or fails to translate, from hospital policy into daily life on the ward.
pmc-13474513:
Al-Nussairi and co-authors built the CardioMetaHybridOptimizer, a feature-selection system that rotates three animal-inspired search algorithms to pick the most informative clinical variables before a neural network judges heart disease risk. Their 2026 framework feeds the chosen features to a CNN-LSTM classifier and was tested on five classic benchmark datasets, from Cleveland to Long Beach VA, with tenfold cross-validation repeated ten times.

The hybrid reached 96.1% classification accuracy, beating standard selectors such as recursive feature elimination and Lasso by 3 to 5% at clear significance across the analysis-of-variance checks. Adaptive switching between the three optimizers, dynamic mutation, and local search cut iteration counts by 30 to 50% against fixed plans. The authors pitch the system as decision support that stays interpretable because doctors can see exactly which biomarkers the model kept.
pmc-13474613:

Kim and colleagues use a Korean cohort to ask whether alcohol's link to liver cancer grows with age. Hepatocellular carcinoma, the liver cancer, is an established cost of heavy drinking, but age specific risk was murky. Their 2026 study follows 3.9 million adults who had a health exam in 2009. It records drinking level and cancer cases over a median of more than eleven years. The analysis splits into twenty year age bands.

Twenty thousand people developed liver cancer in follow up. A dose trend, rising risk with rising intake, reached clear levels only at sixty and over. Heavy drinking raised risk in both the forty to fifty nine band and the sixty plus band. The raise was far larger in the older group, near half again the risk of non drinkers there. Prevention talks, the authors suggest, should press hardest on middle aged and older heavy drinkers.

Karim and colleagues built in 2026 the first zebrafish knockouts of the three ataxin-1 family genes, to learn what these genes do in health. A warped form of one gene causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 1, a brain disease that steals balance and movement. The team cut each gene in turn with CRISPR, a gene editing tool, and tracked growth, movement, and gene activity in the fish.

All three knockouts cut early survival and slowed larval growth a bit. Fish that lacked the first gene moved poorly in light but swam near normal in the dark. Fish that lacked the other two genes were just sluggish overall. As adults, the first group again fared worst on swim tests. Gene readouts in young larvae showed broad shifts tied to nerve growth, immune cell travel, and a light sensing module in the first knockout.

Yang and colleagues reported in 2026 on whether carbon-ion radiotherapy, a treatment using heavy charged particles, can be planned well for melanoma tumors inside the eye. Their software relies on a local effect model, which estimates how strongly the beam affects living tissue. Past clinical success came from a Japanese center using a different dose model, so the two dose scales needed a fair way to be compared.

Yang's team set the conversion factor between the two dose scales at 0.65 for a stated total dose, then checked plans against simulations and real measurements. The checks matched closely, with dose gaps mostly within about 1.6 percent and passing rates of at least 94 percent in their main test. Tumors at least 10 millimetres across could be treated with scan-based planning, supporting wider use of this eye-saving treatment.
